metadata.title: Graph-directed systems and self-similar measures on limit spaces of self-similar groups

extraction_notes.note: The paragraph defining iterated monodromy groups is the argument for the preceding claim that Heicklen-Hoffman follows from Theorem 21 for sub-hyperbolic maps; treated it as a prose proof, so the IMG definition is a proof step (step rule 4) rather than a definition node.

Prose descriptions of computational methods (eigenvector boundary-value method, label-product graph, nucleus-based tile measure) extracted as unmarked algorithms rather than remarks, since later text cites them as methods.

Minor source slips: the proof of Proposition 25 cites Theorem 11 as 'Proposition~\ref{theor_tile_measure}'; Corollary 20 writes $meas(\mathscr{T})$ for $\mu(\mathscr{T})$; the algorithm text calls $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ a left eigenvector although Proposition 3 makes it a right eigenvector; a \ref to Proposition 2 in the proof of Theorem 11 has a line break inside its key and does not resolve, so that edge was added by hand.
The prose proof of Corollary 23 ends with the dangling lead-in 'In particular, we get' directly before the corollary environment.

Introduction restatements of Sections 2-5 results, the abstract, and a few routine side remarks of the Section 3 review (restriction cocycle identity, countability of contracting groups, compactness/connectedness of the limit space, regularity of $\mu$ and $\mathsf{m}$) were not made nodes.

Applications of Nekrashevych's Theorem 6.1.6 in Section 5 state its conclusion in full for the case at hand; kept as external theorem/claim nodes because Propositions 24-25 rely on the map Phi they provide.

nodes.name: Contracting virtual endomorphism
nodes.statement: A virtual endomorphism $\phi$ is contracting if it asymptotically contracts the length of group elements with respect to some generating set.
differentia: asymptotically contracts the length of group elements with respect to some generating set

nodes.name: Self-similar set (attractor of an iterated function system)
nodes.statement: The self-similar set (the attractor) given by the system of contracting similarities $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ (iterated function system) of a complete metric space is the unique compact set $T$ satisfying $T=\cup_{i=1}^n f_i(T)$.
nodes.statement_short: The attractor of an IFS of contracting similarities: the unique compact $T$ with $T=\cup f_i(T)$.

nodes.name: Hutchinson's theorem on self-similar measures
nodes.statement: Given a probability vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, Hutchinson \cite{hutch:fract_self_similarity} showed the existence of a unique probability measure $\mu$ supported on $T$ satisfying \begin{equation} \mu(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i\mu(f_i^{-1}(A)), \mbox{ for any Borel set $A$}, \end{equation} which is called the self-similar measure.
nodes.statement_short: For a probability vector $p$ there is a unique probability measure on the attractor satisfying the self-similarity equation.
assumptions: Given a probability vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)$
conclusions: the existence of a unique probability measure $\mu$ supported on $T$ satisfying

nodes.name: Self-similarity equation for measures
nodes.statement: \mu(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i\mu(f_i^{-1}(A)), \mbox{ for any Borel set $A$},
nodes.label: eqn_self_similar_measure

nodes.name: Finite words $X^*$
nodes.statement: Denote by $X^{*}=\{x_1x_2\ldots x_n | x_i\in X, n\geq 0\}$ the set of all finite words over $X$ (including the empty word denoted $\emptyset$).

nodes.name: Right-infinite sequences $X^\omega$
nodes.statement: Let $X^{\omega}$ be the set of all right-infinite sequences (words) $x_1x_2\ldots$, $x_i\in X$.

nodes.name: Left-infinite sequences $X^{-\omega}$
nodes.statement: Let $X^{-\omega}$ be the set of all left-infinite sequences (words) $\ldots x_2x_1$, $x_i\in X$.

nodes.name: Length of a word
nodes.statement: The length of a word $v=x_1x_2\ldots x_n$ is denoted by $|v| = n$.

nodes.name: Shift on $X^\omega$
nodes.statement: The \textit{shift on the space $X^\omega$} is the map $\sigma:X^\omega\rightarrow X^\omega$, which deletes the first letter of a word, i.e. $\sigma(x_1x_2x_3\ldots) = x_2x_3\ldots$.

nodes.name: Shift on $X^{-\omega}$
nodes.statement: The \textit{shift on the space $X^{-\omega}$} is the map also denoted by $\sigma$, which deletes the last letter of a word, i.e. $\sigma(\ldots x_3x_2x_1) = \ldots x_3x_2$.

nodes.name: Inverse branches $\sigma_x$ of the shift
nodes.statement: The branches $\sigma_x$ for $x\in X$ of the inverse of $\sigma$ are defined by $\sigma_x(x_1x_2\ldots)=xx_1x_2\ldots$ and $\sigma_x(\ldots x_2x_1)=\ldots x_2x_1x$.

nodes.name: Bernoulli measure
nodes.statement: Let $p=(p_x)_{x\in X}$ be a probability vector (fixed for the rest of the section) and let $\mu_p$ be the \textit{Bernoulli measure} on $X^\omega$ with weight $p$, i.e. this measure is defined on cylindrical sets by \[ \mu_p(x_1x_2\ldots x_nX^\omega)=p_{x_1}p_{x_2}\ldots p_{x_n}. \] The measure on $X^{-\omega}$ is defined in the same way.
nodes.statement_short: Product measure $\mu_p$ on $X^\omega$ (and $X^{-\omega}$) giving a cylinder $x_1\ldots x_nX^\omega$ mass $p_{x_1}\cdots p_{x_n}$.

nodes.name: Uniform Bernoulli measure
nodes.statement: In case $p_x=\frac{1}{|X|}$ for all $x\in X$, the measure $\mu_p$ is the \textit{uniform Bernoulli measure} denoted $\mu_u$.

nodes.name: One-sided Bernoulli $|X|$-shift
nodes.statement: The dynamical system $(X^\omega,\sigma,\mu_u)$ is called the \textit{one-sided Bernoulli $|X|$-shift}.

nodes.name: Bernoulli measure is the unique self-similar measure
nodes.statement: The measure $\mu_p$ is the unique regular Borel probability measure on $X^\omega$ that satisfies the self-similarity condition: \[ \mu_p(A)=\sum_{x\in X} p_x\mu_p(\sigma_x^{-1}(A)) \] for any Borel set $A\subset X^\omega$.
assumptions: for any Borel set $A\subset X^\omega$
conclusions: The measure $\mu_p$ is the unique regular Borel probability measure on $X^\omega$ that satisfies the self-similarity condition:

nodes.name: Sequence starting in a vertex
nodes.statement: We say that a sequence $x_1x_2\ldots\in X^\omega$ (a word $x_1x_2\ldots x_n\in X^{*}$) \textit{starts in the vertex $v$} if there exists a right-infinite path $e_1e_2\ldots$ (finite path $e_1e_2\ldots e_n$) in $\Gamma$, which starts in $v$ and is labeled by $x_1x_2\ldots$ (respectively $x_1x_2\ldots x_n$).

nodes.name: Sequence ending in a vertex
nodes.statement: Similarly, we say that a sequence $\ldots x_2x_1\in X^{-\omega}$ (a word $x_n\ldots x_2x_1\in X^{*}$) \textit{ends in the vertex $v$} if there exists a left-infinite path $\ldots e_2e_1$ (finite path $e_n\ldots e_2e_1$) in $\Gamma$, which ends in $v$ and is labeled by $\ldots x_2x_1$ (respectively $x_n\ldots x_2x_1$).

nodes.name: Vertex set $V(w)$
nodes.statement: For every $w\in X^*\cup X^{-\omega}$ denote by $V_\Gamma(w)=V(w)\subset V$ the set of all vertices $v\in V$ such that the sequence $w$ ends in $v$.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of $V(w)$
nodes.statement: Observe that $V(w'w)\subseteq V(w)$ for arbitrary word $w'$ and finite word~$w$.
assumptions: for arbitrary word $w'$ and finite word~$w$
conclusions: $V(w'w)\subseteq V(w)$

nodes.name: Sets $B_v$ and $F_v$
nodes.statement: For every vertex $v\in V$ denote by $B_v$ the set of all right-infinite sequences that start in $v$, and denote by $F_v$ the set of all left-infinite sequences that end in $v$.

nodes.name: Sofic subshifts
nodes.statement: The sets $\mathscr{B}=\cup_{v\in V}B_v$ and $\mathscr{F}=\cup_{v\in V}F_v$ are the one-sided (respectively, right and left) \textit{sofic subshifts} associated with the graph $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Recursion for the sets $F_v$
nodes.statement: The sets $F_v, v\in V$, satisfy the recursion \[ F_v=\bigcup_{u\, \stackrel{x}{\rightarrow} \,v} \sigma_x(F_u) \] (here the union is taken over all edges which end in $v$).
conclusions: The sets $F_v, v\in V$, satisfy the recursion

nodes.name: Graph-directed IFS on the sofic subshift
nodes.statement: Hence, associating the map $\sigma_x$ with every edge $e$ of the graph $\Gamma$ labeled by $x$, the collection of sets $\{F_v, v\in V\}$ can be seen as the graph-directed iterated function system on the sofic subshift $\mathscr{F}$ with the underlying graph $\Gamma$ (see \cite{fractal_gr_sets}). All the maps $\sigma_x^{-1}$ are restrictions of the shift $\sigma$, and thus $\{F_vx, v\in V\}$ is the Markov partition of the dynamical system $(\mathscr{F},\sigma)$. Similarly, the collection of sets $\{B_v, v\in V\}$ can be seen as the graph-directed iterated function system on the sofic subshift~$\mathscr{B}$.
nodes.statement_short: The sets $F_v$ (and $B_v$) form a graph-directed iterated function system on the sofic subshift, with Markov partition $\{F_vx\}$.

nodes.name: Right-resolving graph
nodes.statement: A labeled graph $\Gamma=(V,E)$ is called \textit{right-resolving} (Shannon graph in some terminology) if for every vertex $v\in V$ the edges starting at $v$ have different labels.
differentia: for every vertex $v\in V$ the edges starting at $v$ have different labels

nodes.name: Every sofic subshift has a right-resolving presentation
nodes.statement: Every sofic subshift can be given by a right-resolving graph (see Theorem~3.3.2 in \cite{IntroSymbDyn}).
conclusions: Every sofic subshift can be given by a right-resolving graph

nodes.name: Strictly right-resolving graph
nodes.statement: A right-resolving graph is called \textit{strictly right-resolving} if every vertex $v\in V$ has an outgoing edge labeled by $x$ for every $x\in X$.
differentia: every vertex $v\in V$ has an outgoing edge labeled by $x$ for every $x\in X$

nodes.name: Measure vectors and $\mu_p(\Gamma)$
nodes.statement: For a labeled graph $\Gamma=(V,E)$ we use the following notations: \[ \vec\mu_p(\mathscr{B})=(\mu_p(B_v))_{v\in V}, \quad \vec\mu_p(\mathscr{F})=(\mu_p(F_v))_{v\in V}, \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \mu_p(\Gamma)=\sum_{v\in V} \mu_p(F_v). \]
nodes.statement_short: Vectors of measures $(\mu_p(B_v))_v$, $(\mu_p(F_v))_v$ and the total $\mu_p(\Gamma)=\sum_v\mu_p(F_v)$.

nodes.name: Integrality of the measure of a right-resolving graph
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph. Then \[ \mu_p(\Gamma)=\min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} |V(w)|=\min_{w\in X^*} |V(w)|. \] In particular, the measure $\mu_p(\Gamma)$ is integer.
nodes.statement_short: For a finite right-resolving graph, $\mu_p(\Gamma)$ equals the minimal number of vertices a sequence can end in, hence is an integer.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph.
conclusions: \mu_p(\Gamma)=\min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} |V(w)|=\min_{w\in X^*} |V(w)|.
In particular, the measure $\mu_p(\Gamma)$ is integer.
nodes.label: theor_measure_graph_integer

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Let $w=\ldots x_2x_1\in X^{-\omega}$ and denote $w_n=x_n\ldots x_2x_1$ for $n\geq 1$. Observe, that $V(w)\subseteq V(w_n)$ and $V(w_n)\subseteq V(w_m)$ for $n\geq m$. Take a vertex $v\in \cap_{n\geq 1} V(w_n)$. Let $P_n$ be the set of all paths $e_n\ldots e_2e_1$ labeled by $w_n$ and ending in $v$. The set $P_n$ is a finite non-empty set for every $n$, and $e_{n-1}\ldots e_2e_1\in P_{n-1}$ for every path $e_n\ldots e_2e_1\in P_n$. Since the inverse limit of a sequence of finite non-empty sets is non-empty, there exists a left-infinite path $\ldots e_2e_1$ labeled by $w$ and ending in $v$. Then $v\in V(w)$ and we get \begin{equation} V(w)=\bigcap_{n\geq 1} V(w_n). \end{equation} From this follows that $|V(w)|=\min\limits_{n\geq 1} |V(w_n)|$ for $w\in X^{-\omega}$. Then \[ \min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} |V(w)|=\min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} \min_{n\geq 1} |V(w_n)|=\min_{w\in X^*} |V(w)| \] and the second equality of the theorem is proved. Define the integer $k=\min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} |V(w)|$ and consider the set $\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{O}(\Gamma)\subseteq X^{-\omega}$ of all sequences $w\in X^{-\omega}$ such that $|V(w)|=k$. Define $\mathcal{O}^*$ as the set of finite words that satisfy the same condition. We have the following lemma. \begin{lemma} The set $\mathcal{O}$ is open and dense in $X^{-\omega}$, and $\mu_p(\mathcal{O})=1$. For each $w\in\mathcal{O}$ there is a beginning of $w$ that belongs to $\mathcal{O}^*$. Equivalently, $\mathcal{O}=\cup_{w\in\mathcal{O}^*}X^{-\omega} w$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} If $w\in\mathcal{O}$ then $k=|V(w)|=\min_{n\geq 1} |V(w_n)|$ and there exists $N\geq 1$ such that $|V(w_N)|=k$. Then $k\leq |V(\omega w_N)|\leq |V(w_N)|=k$ for all $\omega\in X^{-\omega}$. Hence $w_N\in\mathcal{O}^*$, $X^{-\omega} w_N\subseteq\mathcal{O}$ and so $\mathcal{O}$ is open, and thus measurable. Let $u\in X^*$ be such that $|V(u)|=k$. Let us show that if $w\in X^{-\omega}$ contains the subword $u$ then $w\in\mathcal{O}$. If $w=w'u$ then $k\leq |V(w'u)|\leq |V(u)|=k$ and $w\in\mathcal{O}$. Observe that $V(ux)$ is the set of those vertices $v\in V$ for which there exists an edge labeled by $x$ which starts in some vertex of $V(u)$ and ends in $v$. Since the graph $\Gamma$ is right-resolving there is no more than one such an edge for each vertex of $V(u)$, and thus $|V(ux)|\leq |V(u)|$. It implies that if $w=w'uu'$ than $k\leq |V(w)|\leq |V(u)|=k$ and thus $|V(w)|=k$, so $w\in\mathcal{O}$. The Bernoulli measure of the set of all words $w'uu', u'\in X^*, w'\in X^{-\omega}$, is equal to $1$. Thus $\mu_p(\mathcal{O})=1$. It follows also that $\mathcal{O}$ is dense in $X^{-\omega}$. \end{proof} By construction of the set $\mathcal{O}$ for every $w\in\mathcal{O}$ there exist exactly $k$ vertices $v$ such that $w\in F_v$. Let $\chi_{F_v}$ be the characteristic function of the set $F_v$. Then $\sum_{v\in V}\chi_{F_v}=k$ almost everywhere. Integrating we get $\mu_p(\Gamma)=\sum\limits_{v\in V} \mu_p(F_v)=k$.
nodes.statement_short: Compactness (inverse limit) gives $V(w)=\cap V(w_n)$; then the set of sequences ending in exactly $k$ vertices has full measure, so integrating gives $\mu_p(\Gamma)=k$.

nodes.name: $V(w)$ as intersection of $V(w_n)$
nodes.statement: V(w)=\bigcap_{n\geq 1} V(w_n).
nodes.label: eqn_th1_V(w) eq cap V(w_n)

nodes.name: The set $\mathcal{O}$ is open, dense and of full measure
nodes.statement: The set $\mathcal{O}$ is open and dense in $X^{-\omega}$, and $\mu_p(\mathcal{O})=1$. For each $w\in\mathcal{O}$ there is a beginning of $w$ that belongs to $\mathcal{O}^*$. Equivalently, $\mathcal{O}=\cup_{w\in\mathcal{O}^*}X^{-\omega} w$.
nodes.statement_short: The sequences ending in the minimal number of vertices form an open dense full-measure set, a union of cylinders.
conclusions: The set $\mathcal{O}$ is open and dense in $X^{-\omega}$, and $\mu_p(\mathcal{O})=1$.
For each $w\in\mathcal{O}$ there is a beginning of $w$ that belongs to $\mathcal{O}^*$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: If $w\in\mathcal{O}$ then $k=|V(w)|=\min_{n\geq 1} |V(w_n)|$ and there exists $N\geq 1$ such that $|V(w_N)|=k$. Then $k\leq |V(\omega w_N)|\leq |V(w_N)|=k$ for all $\omega\in X^{-\omega}$. Hence $w_N\in\mathcal{O}^*$, $X^{-\omega} w_N\subseteq\mathcal{O}$ and so $\mathcal{O}$ is open, and thus measurable. Let $u\in X^*$ be such that $|V(u)|=k$. Let us show that if $w\in X^{-\omega}$ contains the subword $u$ then $w\in\mathcal{O}$. If $w=w'u$ then $k\leq |V(w'u)|\leq |V(u)|=k$ and $w\in\mathcal{O}$. Observe that $V(ux)$ is the set of those vertices $v\in V$ for which there exists an edge labeled by $x$ which starts in some vertex of $V(u)$ and ends in $v$. Since the graph $\Gamma$ is right-resolving there is no more than one such an edge for each vertex of $V(u)$, and thus $|V(ux)|\leq |V(u)|$. It implies that if $w=w'uu'$ than $k\leq |V(w)|\leq |V(u)|=k$ and thus $|V(w)|=k$, so $w\in\mathcal{O}$. The Bernoulli measure of the set of all words $w'uu', u'\in X^*, w'\in X^{-\omega}$, is equal to $1$. Thus $\mu_p(\mathcal{O})=1$. It follows also that $\mathcal{O}$ is dense in $X^{-\omega}$.
nodes.statement_short: A synchronizing word $u$ with $|V(u)|=k$: every sequence containing $u$ lies in $\mathcal{O}$ since right-resolving graphs do not increase $|V|$, and a.e. sequence contains $u$.

nodes.name: Theorem 1 beyond Bernoulli measures
nodes.statement: The theorem holds not only for Bernoulli measures. The only property that was used is that for every word $u\in X^{*}$ the set of all words, which contain $u$ as a subword, has measure $1$. It should be pointed out that the number $\mu(\Gamma)$ is independent on the chosen measure $\mu$, while the measures $\mu(F_v)$, $\mu(B_v)$ and $\sum_{v\in V} \mu(B_v)$ depend on $\mu$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1 holds for any measure giving full mass to sequences containing each fixed word; $\mu(\Gamma)$ is measure-independent.

nodes.name: Measure number of a graph
nodes.statement: The number $meas(\Gamma)=\mu_p(\Gamma)$ is called the \textit{measure number} of the graph~$\Gamma$.

nodes.name: A.e. sequence ends in $meas(\Gamma)$ vertices
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{theor_measure_graph_integer} shows that almost every sequence $w\in X^{-\omega}$ ends in precisely $meas(\Gamma)$ vertices of $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Full right subshift iff full left subshift
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite labeled graph. Then $\mathscr{B}=X^\omega$ if and only if $\mathscr{F}=X^{-\omega}$. In particular, $\mathscr{F}=X^{-\omega}$ for a finite strictly right-resolving graph $\Gamma$.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite labeled graph.
conclusions: $\mathscr{B}=X^\omega$ if and only if $\mathscr{F}=X^{-\omega}$.
$\mathscr{F}=X^{-\omega}$ for a finite strictly right-resolving graph $\Gamma$.
nodes.label: prop cup B_v eq cup F_v

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: Since the inverse limit of nonempty finite sets is nonempty, $\mathscr{B}=X^\omega$ ($\mathscr{F}=X^{-\omega}$) is equivalent to the fact that every finite word $v\in{X^*}$ labels some path in $\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Compactness: both conditions are equivalent to every finite word labelling a path.

nodes.name: Adjacency matrix
nodes.statement: The matrix $A=(a_{vu})_{v,u\in V}$, where $a_{vu}$ is equal to the number of edges from $v$ to $u$, is the \textit{adjacency matrix} of the graph $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Matrix $T_p$
nodes.statement: For the probability vector $p=(p_x)_{x\in X}$ define the matrix \[ T_p=(t_{vu})_{v,u\in V}, \mbox{ where } t_{vu}=\sum\limits_{v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u}p_x \] (the sum is taken over all edges from $v$ to $u$).
nodes.statement_short: $T_p$ has entry $t_{vu}$ equal to the total weight $\sum p_x$ of edges from $v$ to $u$.

nodes.name: Irreducibility iff strong connectivity
nodes.statement: The matrices $A$ and $T_p$ are irreducible if and only if the graph $\Gamma$ is strongly connected.
conclusions: The matrices $A$ and $T_p$ are irreducible if and only if the graph $\Gamma$ is strongly connected.

nodes.name: Transition matrix
nodes.statement: If the graph $\Gamma$ is right-resolving, then the matrix $T_p$ is the \textit{transition matrix} of the random walk on the weighted directed graph $\Gamma$, where each edge labeled by $x$ has weight $p_x$.

nodes.name: Spectral radius bounds for right-resolving graphs
nodes.statement: In this case the row sums of the matrix $A$ are $\leq |X|$, and the row sums of the matrix $T_p$ are $\leq 1$, hence the spectral radius of $A$ is $\leq |X|$, and the spectral radius of $T_p$ is $\leq 1$. If the graph $\Gamma$ is strictly right-resolving, then the transition matrix $T_p$ is right stochastic.
nodes.statement_short: For right-resolving graphs, $A$ has spectral radius at most $|X|$ and $T_p$ at most 1; strictly right-resolving makes $T_p$ stochastic.

nodes.name: Measure vectors are eigenvectors of the transition matrix
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph with the transition matrix~$T_p$. If the vector $\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ is nonzero then it is the right eigenvector of $T_p$ for the eigenvalue~$1$. If the vector $\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ is nonzero then it is the left eigenvector of $T_p$ for the eigenvalue~$1$.
nodes.statement_short: For right-resolving graphs, the nonzero vectors $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ and $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ are right/left eigenvectors of $T_p$ for eigenvalue 1.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph with the transition matrix~$T_p$.
If the vector $\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ is nonzero

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: By construction, for every vertex $v\in V$ we have \[ B_v=\bigsqcup_{v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u} xB_u \] (here the union is disjoint because the graph $\Gamma$ is right-resolving). It implies \[ \mu_p(B_v)=\sum_{v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u} p_x\mu_p(B_{u})=\sum_{u\in V} t_{vu}\mu_p(B_{u}). \] Thus the nonzero vector $\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ is the right eigenvector of $T_p$ for the eigenvalue~$1$. Similarly, \[ F_v=\bigcup_{u\stackrel{x}\rightarrow v} F_{u}x,\ v\in V, \] and, since the graph $\Gamma$ is right-resolving, that implies \begin{equation*} \mu_p(F_v)\leq\sum_{u\stackrel{x}\rightarrow v} p_x\mu_p(F_{u})=\sum_{u\in V} t_{uv}\mu_p(F_{u})\quad \Rightarrow\quad \vec \mu_p(\mathscr{F})\leq\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{F}) T_p. \end{equation*} The standard arguments based on the theory of nonnegative matrices (see for example \cite[proof of Theorem 4.5]{he_hui:self_affine}, \cite[p. 197]{gab_yu:natur_til}, \cite{handbook:rothblum}) end the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Disjoint decomposition $B_v=\sqcup xB_u$ gives the right eigen-equation; the analogous inequality for $F_v$ plus Perron-Frobenius theory of nonnegative matrices finishes.

nodes.name: Measure number is additive over strictly right-resolving components
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph. Let $\{\Gamma_i\}$ be the set of all strongly connected components of $\Gamma$, which are strictly right-resolving graphs. Then $meas(\Gamma)=\sum_imeas(\Gamma_i)$.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph.
Let $\{\Gamma_i\}$ be the set of all strongly connected components of $\Gamma$, which are strictly right-resolving graphs.
conclusions: $meas(\Gamma)=\sum_imeas(\Gamma_i)$.
nodes.label: cor_meas_sum_meas

nodes.name: Open set condition for graphs gives measure number 1
nodes.statement: In particular, if a finite strictly right-resolving graph $\Gamma$ contains a vertex $v_0$ such that for each vertex $v$ there is a path in $\Gamma$ from $v$ to $v_0$ and for each $x\in X$ there is an edge from $v_0$ to $v_0$ labeled by $x$ (the open set condition for graphs), then $meas(\Gamma)=1$.
assumptions: a finite strictly right-resolving graph $\Gamma$ contains a vertex $v_0$ such that for each vertex $v$ there is a path in $\Gamma$ from $v$ to $v_0$ and for each $x\in X$ there is an edge from $v_0$ to $v_0$ labeled by $x$
conclusions: $meas(\Gamma)=1$

nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph with the adjacency matrix~$A$. For the uniform Bernoulli measure $\mu_u$ the nonzero vectors $\vec \mu_u(\mathscr{B})$ and $\vec \mu_u(\mathscr{F})$ are respectively the right and left eigenvectors of $A$ for the eigenvalue $|X|$.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph with the adjacency matrix~$A$.
conclusions: the nonzero vectors $\vec \mu_u(\mathscr{B})$ and $\vec \mu_u(\mathscr{F})$ are respectively the right and left eigenvectors of $A$ for the eigenvalue $|X|$.

nodes.name: Non-right-resolving graph with non-integer measure
nodes.statement: For the graph $\Gamma$ shown in Figure~\ref{fig_Example_3_Graphs} we get $F_a=X^{-\omega} 0$, $F_b=X^{-\omega}$, the vector $\vec\mu_u(\mathscr{F})=(1/2,1)$ is not an eigenvector of the adjacency matrix, and $\mu_u(\Gamma)=3/2$.

nodes.name: Same transition matrix, different measure numbers
nodes.statement: Consider two graphs $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ shown in Figure~\ref{fig_Example_3_Graphs}. They have the same transition matrix (for the uniform Bernoulli measure), however $F_{a_1}=F_{b_1}=X^{-\omega}$ and $F_{a_2}=X^{-\omega} 0$, $F_{b_2}=X^{-\omega} 1$. Hence, $\mu_u(\Gamma_1)=2$ and $\mu_u(\Gamma_2)=1$.

nodes.name: Reduction to strictly right-resolving strongly connected components
nodes.statement: Although Theorem~\ref{theor_measure_graph_integer} gives a usefull characterization of the number $\mu_p(\Gamma)$, it does not present an algorithmic way to find it. It follows from Proposition~\ref{prop_eigenvect_transition_matr} that the problem of finding $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ and $\mu_p(\Gamma)$ reduces to the strongly connected components which are strictly right-resolving graphs (for all other vertices $\mu_p(F_v)=0$). Notice that if $\Gamma$ is a strongly connected strictly right-resolving graph, then the vector $\frac{1}{\mu_p(\Gamma)}\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ is the unique stationary probability distribution of the stochastic matrix $T_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Computing $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ reduces to strictly right-resolving strongly connected components, where it is a multiple of the stationary distribution of $T_p$.

nodes.name: Computing $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ for a right-resolving graph
nodes.statement: At the same time Proposition~\ref{prop_eigenvect_transition_matr} implies the algorithm to find the vector $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ for a right-resolving graph. Indeed, a left eigenvector of $T_p$ for the eigenvalue $1$ is uniquely defined if we know its entries $\mu_p(B_v)$ for vertices $v$ in the strongly connected components of $\Gamma$ without outgoing edges. For every such a component $\Gamma'$, we have $B_v=X^\omega$ and $\mu_p(B_v)=1$ for every vertex $v\in\Gamma'$ if the component $\Gamma'$ is a strictly right-resolving graph, and $\mu_p(B_v)=0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the boundary values $\mu_p(B_v)\in\{0,1\}$ on sink components (1 iff strictly right-resolving), then solve the eigenvector equation for $T_p$ with eigenvalue 1.

nodes.name: Rational transition matrix gives rational measures
nodes.statement: In particular, if the matrix $T_p$ is rational then the values $\mu_p(B_v)$ are rational.
assumptions: if the matrix $T_p$ is rational
conclusions: the values $\mu_p(B_v)$ are rational

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Proposition 6 (subset construction)
nodes.statement: Given a finite labeled graph $\Gamma=(V,E)$ the problems of finding the measures $\mu_p(B_v)$ and $\mu_p(F_v)$ are equivalent, and can be reduced to right-resolving graphs. The problem is that the system \[ B_v=\bigcup_{v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u} xB_{u}=\bigsqcup_{x\in X}x\left(\bigcup_{v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u} B_{u}\right),\ v\in V \] is not self-similar in the sense that the above expression involves not only the sets $B_v$ but also their finite unions. Introducing additional terms to this recursion corresponding to these unions we get a system with a right-resolving graph. This procedure is similar to the construction described in the proof of Theorem~3.3.2 in \cite{IntroSymbDyn}.
nodes.statement_short: Subset construction: add vertices for the finite unions of the $B_u$ appearing in the recursion, as in Lind-Marcus Thm 3.3.2.

nodes.name: Reduction of any graph to a right-resolving graph
nodes.statement: For every finite graph $\Gamma=(V,E)$ one can construct a finite right-resolving graph $\Gamma'=(V',E')$ with the property that for every $v\in V$ there exists $v'\in V'$ such that $B_v=B_{v'}$.
assumptions: For every finite graph $\Gamma=(V,E)$
conclusions: one can construct a finite right-resolving graph $\Gamma'=(V',E')$ with the property that for every $v\in V$ there exists $v'\in V'$ such that $B_v=B_{v'}$.

nodes.name: Measures of the subshifts
nodes.statement: Similarly, one can find the measures of subshifts $\mathscr{B}$ and $\mathscr{F}$ by introducing new vertices corresponding to $\cup_{v\in V} B_v$ and $\cup_{v\in V} F_v$.

nodes.name: Rationality of uniform measures
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite labeled graph. For the uniform Bernoulli measure $\mu_u$ all measures $\mu_u(B_v)$, $\mu_u(F_v)$, $\mu_u(\Gamma)$ are rational.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite labeled graph.
conclusions: For the uniform Bernoulli measure $\mu_u$ all measures $\mu_u(B_v)$, $\mu_u(F_v)$, $\mu_u(\Gamma)$ are rational.
nodes.label: cor_meas_gr_rational

nodes.name: Measure of intersections $B_v\cap B_u$ via the label product graph
nodes.statement: Consider the question how to find the measure of the intersection $B_v\cap B_u$ for $v,u\in V$. Construct a new graph $\mathscr{G}$ with the set of vertices $V\times V$ and put an edge from $(v,u)$ to $(v',u')$ labeled by $x\in X$ for every edges $v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow v'$ and $u\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u'$ in the graph $\Gamma$ (label products of graphs by Definition~3.4.8 in \cite{IntroSymbDyn}). It is easy to see that then $B_{(v,u)}=B_v\cap B_u$ (see Proposition~3.4.10 in \cite{IntroSymbDyn}).
nodes.statement_short: Form the label product graph on $V\times V$; its sets $B_{(v,u)}$ are the intersections $B_v\cap B_u$, whose measures are then computed as before.
output: the measure of the intersection $B_v\cap B_u$

nodes.name: Graphs labelled by words
nodes.statement: The described methods work in a more general case when labels are words over $X$. Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a directed graph labeled by labels from $X^{*}\setminus\{\emptyset\}$. Define the sets $B_v$ and $F_v$ for $v\in V$ as above. Similarly, the collection of sets $\{B_v, v\in V\}$ can be seen as the graph-directed function system with the underlying graph $\Gamma$, where the map $\sigma_{x_1\ldots x_n}=\sigma_{x_n}\circ\ldots\circ\sigma_{x_1}$ is associated with every edge labeled by $x_1\ldots x_n$. To find the measures of the sets $B_v$ and $F_v$, we can replace each edge labeled by a word $x_1x_2\ldots x_k$ by a sequence of edges labeled by letters $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k$, and apply the above method to this new graph. Also we can directly use Proposition~\ref{prop_eigenvect_transition_matr}, where such graph $\Gamma$ is called \textit{right-resolving} if for every vertex $v\in V$ the word-label of an edge starting at $v$ is not a prefix of the word-label of another edge starting at $v$ (i.e. in some sense the associated automaton is deterministic). The transition matrix $T_p$ is defined similarly \[ T_p=(t_{vu})_{v,u\in V}, \mbox{ where } t_{vu}=\sum\limits_{v\xrightarrow{x_1...x_k} u}p_{x_1}p_{x_2}\ldots p_{x_k}. \]
nodes.statement_short: The methods extend to graphs labelled by nonempty words, by subdividing edges or by a prefix-free notion of right-resolving and a weighted $T_p$.

nodes.name: Self-similar action
nodes.statement: A faithful action of a group $G$ on the set $X^*$ is called \emph{self-similar} if for every $g\in G$ and $x\in X$ there exist $h\in G$ and $y\in X$ such that \[ g(xw)=yh(w) \] for all $w\in X^*$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.genus: faithful action of a group $G$ on the set $X^*$
differentia: for every $g\in G$ and $x\in X$ there exist $h\in G$ and $y\in X$ such that

nodes.name: Restriction $g|_x$
nodes.statement: The element $h$ is called the \textit{restriction} of $g$ on $x$ and denoted $h=g|_x$. Inductively one defines the restriction $g|_{x_1x_2\ldots x_n}=g|_{x_1}|_{x_2}\ldots |_{x_n}$ for every word $x_1\ldots x_n\in X^n$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Virtual endomorphism
nodes.statement: The study of the self-similar actions of a group is in some sense the study of the \textit{virtual endomorphisms} of this group, which are homomorphisms from a subgroup of finite index to the group.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
differentia: from a subgroup of finite index to the group

nodes.name: Coset transversal and cocycle
nodes.statement: Let $\phi: H\rightarrow G$ be a virtual endomorphism of the group $G$, where $H<G$ is a subgroup of index $d$. Let us choose a left coset transversal $T=\{g_0,g_1,\ldots,g_{d-1}\}$ for the subgroup $H$, and a sequence $C=\{h_0,h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1}\}$ of elements of $G$ called a \emph{cocycle}.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Self-similar action defined by a triple $(\phi,T,C)$
nodes.statement: The self-similar action $(G,X^{*})$ with the alphabet $X=\{x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_{d-1}\}$ defined by the triple $(\phi,T,C)$ is given by \[ g(x_i)=x_j,\qquad g|_{x_i}=h_j^{-1}\phi(g_j^{-1}gg_i)h_i, \] where $j$ is such that $g_j^{-1}gg_i\in H$ (such $j$ is unique).
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.statement_short: $g(x_i)=x_j$ and $g|_{x_i}=h_j^{-1}\phi(g_j^{-1}gg_i)h_i$ where $g_j^{-1}gg_i\in H$.
nodes.definiendum: self-similar action defined by the triple $(\phi,T,C)$

nodes.name: Every self-similar action arises from a triple
nodes.statement: Conversely, every self-similar action can be obtained in this way.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
conclusions: every self-similar action can be obtained in this way

nodes.name: A self-similar action $(G,X^*)$ and a letter $x$
nodes.statement: Let $(G,X^{*})$ be a self-similar action and take a letter $x\in X$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Virtual endomorphism associated to a self-similar action
nodes.statement: Then the map $\phi_x: g\mapsto g|_x$ is a homomorphism from $St_G(x)$ to $G$ called \emph{the virtual endomorphism associated to the self-similar action}.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.definiendum:
the virtual endomorphism associated to the
self-similar action

nodes.name: Actions with the same virtual endomorphism are conjugate
nodes.statement: Different self-similar actions of the group $G$ with the same associated virtual endomorphism are conjugated by Proposition~2.3.4 in \cite{self_sim_groups}.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
conclusions: Different self-similar actions of the group $G$ with the same associated virtual endomorphism are conjugated

nodes.name: Contracting self-similar action
nodes.statement: A self-similar action of a group $G$ is called \emph{contracting} if there exists a finite set $\mathcal{N}$ such that for every $g\in G$ there exists $k\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $g|_v\in\mathcal{N}$ for all words $v\in X^*$ of length $\geq k$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
differentia: there exists a finite set $\mathcal{N}$ such that for every $g\in G$ there exists $k\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $g|_v\in\mathcal{N}$ for all words $v\in X^*$ of length $\geq k$

nodes.name: Nucleus
nodes.statement: The smallest set $\mathcal{N}$ with this property is called the \emph{nucleus} of the self-similar action.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Moore diagram of the nucleus
nodes.statement: It can be represented by the \textit{Moore diagram}, which is the directed labeled graph with the set of vertices $\mathcal{N}$, where there is an edge from $g$ to $g|_x$ labeled $(x,g(x))$ for every $x\in X$ and $g\in\mathcal{N}$. We identify the nucleus with its Moore diagram, also denoted by $\mathcal{N}$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
differentia: with the set of vertices $\mathcal{N}$, where there is an edge from $g$ to $g|_x$ labeled $(x,g(x))$ for every $x\in X$ and $g\in\mathcal{N}$

nodes.name: Contraction depends only on the virtual endomorphism
nodes.statement: The contracting property of the action depends only on the virtual endomorphism but not on the chosen coset transversal and cocycle (see Corollary~2.11.7 in \cite{self_sim_groups}).
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Asymptotic equivalence
nodes.statement: Two elements $\ldots x_2x_1\cdot g$ and $\ldots y_2y_1\cdot h$ of $X^{-\omega}\times G$ are called \textit{asymptotically equivalent} if there exist a finite set $K\subset G$ and a sequence $g_n\in K, n\geq 1,$ such that \begin{displaymath} g_n(x_n x_{n-1}\ldots x_1)=y_n y_{n-1}\ldots y_1\qquad \mbox{ and }\qquad g_n|_{x_n x_{n-1}\ldots x_1}\cdot g=h \end{displaymath} for every $n\geq 1$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.statement_short: $\ldots x_2x_1\cdot g\sim\ldots y_2y_1\cdot h$ if a bounded sequence $g_n$ maps $x_n\ldots x_1$ to $y_n\ldots y_1$ with $g_n|_{x_n\ldots x_1}g=h$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic equivalence via paths in the nucleus
nodes.statement: Two elements $\ldots x_2x_1\cdot g$ and $\ldots y_2y_1\cdot h$ of $X^{-\omega}\times G$ are asymptotically equivalent if and only if there exists a left-infinite path $\ldots e_2e_1$ in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ ending in the vertex $hg^{-1}$ such that the edge $e_i$ is labeled by $(x_i,y_i)$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
conclusions: Two elements $\ldots x_2x_1\cdot g$ and $\ldots y_2y_1\cdot h$ of $X^{-\omega}\times G$ are asymptotically equivalent if and only if there exists a left-infinite path $\ldots e_2e_1$ in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ ending in the vertex $hg^{-1}$ such that the edge $e_i$ is labeled by $(x_i,y_i)$.
nodes.label: prop_asympt_Moore_diagr

nodes.name: Limit $G$-space
nodes.statement: The quotient of the set $X^{-\omega}\times G$ by the asymptotic equivalence relation is called the \textit{limit $G$-space} of the action and denoted $\limGs[(G,X^*)]$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Maps $\tau_x$ on the limit $G$-space
nodes.statement: The map $\tau_x$ defined by the formula \[ \tau_x(\ldots x_2 x_1\cdot g)=\ldots x_2 x_1 g(x)\cdot g|_x \] is a well-defined continuous map on the limit $G$-space $\limGs$ for every $x\in X$, which is not a homeomorphism in general. Inductively one defines $\tau_{x_1x_2\ldots x_n}=\tau_{x_n}\circ\tau_{x_{n-1}}\circ\ldots\circ\tau_{x_1}$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: (Digit) tile
nodes.statement: The image of $X^{-\omega}\times 1$ in $\limGs$ is called the \textit{(digit) tile} $\mathscr{T}$ of the action.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Tiles $\mathscr{T}_v$
nodes.statement: The image of $X^{-\omega} v\times 1$ for $v\in X^n$ is called the \textit{tile} $\mathscr{T}_v$, equivalently $\mathscr{T}_v=\tau_v(\mathscr{T})$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Tiles cover the limit $G$-space
nodes.statement: It follows directly from definition that \[ \limGs=\bigcup_{g\in G} \mathscr{T}\cdot g \ \ \ \ \mbox{ and } \ \ \ \ \mathscr{T}=\bigcup_{v\in X^n} \mathscr{T}_v. \]
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Intersection criterion for tiles
nodes.statement: Two tiles $\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ and $\mathscr{T}\cdot h$ intersect if and only if $gh^{-1}\in\mathcal{N}$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
conclusions: Two tiles $\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ and $\mathscr{T}\cdot h$ intersect if and only if $gh^{-1}\in\mathcal{N}$.

nodes.name: Open set condition
nodes.statement: A contracting action $(G,X^*)$ satisfies the \emph{open set condition} if for any element $g$ of the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ there exists a word $v\in X^*$ such that $g|_v=1$, i.e. in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ there is a path from any vertex to the trivial state.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Tiles under the open set condition
nodes.statement: If the action satisfies the open set condition then the tile $\mathscr{T}$ is the closure of its interior, and any two different tiles have disjoint interiors; otherwise every tile $\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ is covered by the other tiles (see Proposition~3.3.7 in \cite{self_sim_groups}).
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
assumptions: If the action satisfies the open set condition
conclusions: the tile $\mathscr{T}$ is the closure of its interior, and any two different tiles have disjoint interiors
otherwise every tile $\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ is covered by the other tiles

nodes.name: Limit $G$-space depends only on the virtual endomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $\phi: H\rightarrow G$ be a virtual endomorphism of the group $G$. Let $(G,X^*)$ and $(G,Y^*)$ be the contracting self-similar actions defined respectively by the triples $(\phi,T,C)$ and $(\phi,T',C')$. Then $\limGs[(G,X^*)]$ and $\limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ are homeomorphic and the homeomorphism is the map $\alpha : \limGs[(G,X^*)] \longrightarrow \limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ such that \[ \alpha(\tau_x(t))=\tau_y(\alpha(t))\cdot s_x,\ \mbox{ for }\ t\in \limGs[(G,X^*)], \] where $s_x={h'}_y^{-1}\phi({g'}_y^{-1}g_x)h_x$ and $y$ is such that $g'_yg_x^{-1}\in H$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.statement_short: Actions from triples with the same $\phi$ have homeomorphic limit $G$-spaces via an explicit map $\alpha$ intertwining the $\tau_x$.
assumptions: Let $\phi: H\rightarrow G$ be a virtual endomorphism of the group $G$.
Let $(G,X^*)$ and $(G,Y^*)$ be the contracting self-similar actions defined respectively by the triples $(\phi,T,C)$ and $(\phi,T',C')$.
conclusions: Then $\limGs[(G,X^*)]$ and $\limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ are homeomorphic
nodes.label: theor_limsX hom limsY

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9 (by reference)
nodes.statement: The statement follows from Sections~2.1--2.5 in \cite{self_sim_groups}.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.statement_short: Follows from Nekrashevych's monograph, Sections 2.1-2.5.

nodes.name: Limit space $\mathscr{J}_G$
nodes.statement: The factor of the limit $G$-space $\limGs$ by the action of the group $G$ is called the \textit{limit space} $\lims=\lims(\phi)$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Limit space as a quotient of $X^{-\omega}$
nodes.statement: It follows from the definition that we may also consider $\lims$ as a factor of $X^{-\omega}$ by the following equivalence relation: two left-infinite sequences $\ldots x_2 x_1,\ldots y_2 y_1$ are equivalent if and only if there exists a left-infinite path $\ldots e_2 e_1$ in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ such that the edge $e_i$ is labeled by $(x_i,y_i)$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Shift map $\mathsf{s}$ on the limit space
nodes.statement: The equivalence relation on $X^{-\omega}$ is invariant under the shift $\sigma$, therefore $\sigma$ induces a continuous surjective map $\mathsf{s}:\lims\rightarrow\lims$, and every point of $\lims$ has at most $|X|$ preimages under $\mathsf{s}$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Limit dynamical system
nodes.statement: The dynamical system $(\lims,\mathsf{s})$ is called the \textit{limit dynamical system} of the self-similar action.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Tiles $\mathsf{T}_v$ of the limit space
nodes.statement: The image of $X^{-\omega} v$ for $v\in X^{n}$ in $\lims$ is called the \textit{tile} $\mathsf{T}_v$ of the $n$-th level.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Recursive structure of tiles $\mathsf{T}_v$
nodes.statement: Clearly \[ \mathsf{T}_v=\bigcup_{x\in X}\mathsf{T}_{xv}\qquad\mbox{ and }\qquad \mathsf{s}(\mathsf{T}_{vx})=\mathsf{T}_v \] for every $v\in X^{*}$ and $x\in X$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Intersection criterion for tiles $\mathsf{T}_v$
nodes.statement: Two tiles $\mathsf{T}_v$ and $\mathsf{T}_u$ of the same level have nonempty intersection if and only if there exists $h\in\mathcal{N}$ such that $h(v)=u$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Tiles of the limit space under the open set condition
nodes.statement: Under the open set condition, every tile $\mathsf{T}_v$ is the closure of its interior, and any two different tiles of the same level have disjoint interiors (Proposition~3.6.5 in \cite{self_sim_groups}).
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
assumptions: Under the open set condition
conclusions: every tile $\mathsf{T}_v$ is the closure of its interior, and any two different tiles of the same level have disjoint interiors

nodes.name: Diameters of tiles tend to zero
nodes.statement: \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \max_{v\in X^n} \rm{diam} (\mathsf{T}_v)=0
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.label: eqn_diam_tile_goes_zero

nodes.name: Limit solenoid
nodes.statement: The inverse limit of the topological spaces $\lims\stackrel{\mathsf{s}}{\leftarrow} \lims \stackrel{\mathsf{s}}{\leftarrow} \cdots$ is called the \textit{limit solenoid} $\sol$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Limit solenoid as a quotient of $X^{\mathbb{Z}}$
nodes.statement: One can consider $\sol$ as a factor of the space $X^{\mathbb{Z}}$ of two-sided infinite sequences by the equivalence relation, where two sequences $\xi,\eta$ are equivalent if and only if there exist a two-sided infinite path in the nucleus labeled by the pair $(\xi,\eta)$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Homeomorphism $\mathsf{e}$ of the solenoid
nodes.statement: The two-sided shift on $X^{\mathbb{Z}}$ induces a homeomorphism $\mathsf{e}:\sol\rightarrow\sol$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Binary adding machine
nodes.statement: Consider the transformation $a$ of the space $X^{*}$ over the binary alphabet $X=\{0,1\}$ defined recursively by the rule \begin{eqnarray*} a(0w)=1w \quad \mbox{ and }\quad a(1w)=0a(w) \end{eqnarray*} for $w\in X^{*}$. The action of $a$ on the space $X^{*}$ corresponds to addition of one in the binary numeration system, and therefore the transformation $a$ is called the (binary) \textit{adding machine}. Indeed, $a(x_1x_2\ldots x_n)=y_1y_2\ldots y_n$ for $x_i,y_i\in X$ if and only if \[ 1+x_1+2x_2+\ldots +2^{n-1}x_n=y_1+2y_2+\ldots+2^{n-1}y_n \mod 2^{n}. \] \begin{figure} \begin{center} \psfrag{a}{$a$} \psfrag{a1}{$a^{-1}$} \psfrag{id}{$id$} \psfrag{00}{$(0,0)$} \psfrag{11}{$(1,1)$} \psfrag{01}{$(0,1)$} \psfrag{10}{$(1,0)$} \epsfig{file=fig2.eps,height=110pt}\caption{The nucleus of the adding machine} \end{center} \end{figure} The group generated by $a$ is the infinite cyclic group, and we have a self-similar action of the group $\mathbb{Z}\cong\langle a\rangle$ on the space $X^{*}$. This action corresponds to the virtual endomorphism $\phi:2\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$ given by $\phi(m)=m/2$ and the coset transversal $T=\{0,1\}$ (there is no need to specify the cocycle for abelian groups). The nucleus of the action $(\mathbb{Z},X^{*})$ is shown in Figure~\ref{fig_AddingMachine}. It follows that two sequences in $X^{-\omega}\times \mathbb{Z}$ are asymptotically equivalent if and only if they are of the form \[ \ldots 000\cdot a^{n+1} \approx \ldots 111\cdot a^n \quad \mbox{or} \quad \ldots 001w\cdot a^n \approx \ldots 110w\cdot a^n \] for $w\in X^{*}$ and $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. This is the usual identification of binary expansions of real numbers (but written to the left). Hence the map $\Phi$ given by the rule \[ \Phi(\ldots x_2x_1\cdot a^n)=n+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \frac{x_i}{2^i},\quad x_i\in X \mbox{ and } n\in\mathbb{Z}, \] induces a homeomorphism between the limit $G$-space $\limGs[(\mathbb{Z},X^{*})]$ and the real line $\mathbb{R}$ with the standard action of $\mathbb{Z}$ by translations. The image of the tile $\mathscr{T}$ under $\Phi$ is the unit interval $[0,1]$. The limit space $\lims[(\mathbb{Z},X^{*})]$ is homeomorphic to the unit circle.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.statement_short: The adding machine generates $\mathbb{Z}$ acting on binary words; its limit $G$-space is $\mathbb{R}$, tile $[0,1]$, limit space the circle.

nodes.name: Measure $\mu$ on the limit $G$-space
nodes.statement: We consider the uniform Bernoulli measure $\mu_u$ on the space $X^{-\omega}$ and the counting measure on the group $G$, and we put the product measure on the space $X^{-\omega}\times G$. The push-forward of this measure under the factor map $\pi_{\limGs[]}:X^{-\omega}\times G\rightarrow\limGs$ defines the \textit{measure $\mu$ on the limit $G$-space} $\limGs$.
nodes.statement_short: Push-forward to the limit $G$-space of uniform Bernoulli $\times$ counting measure on $X^{-\omega}\times G$.

nodes.name: Self-similarity properties of tile measures
nodes.statement: The measures of tiles have the following properties. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mu(\mathscr{T}_v)= |X|^n\cdot\mu(\mathscr{T}_{uv})$ for every $v\in X^{*}$ and $u\in X^n$. \item $\mu(\mathscr{T}_v\cap\mathscr{T}_{v'})=0$ for $v,v'\in X^n, v\neq v'$. \item Let $\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}$ be the measure $\mu$ restricted to the tile $\mathscr{T}$. Then \[ \mu|_{\mathscr{T}}(A)=\sum_{x\in X} \frac{1}{|X|}\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}(\tau_x^{-1}(A)) \] for any Borel set $A\subset\mathscr{T}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Tile measures scale by $|X|^{-n}$ under level-$n$ subdivision, distinct same-level tiles overlap in measure zero, and $\mu|_\mathscr{T}$ is self-similar under the $\tau_x$.
conclusions: $\mu(\mathscr{T}_v)= |X|^n\cdot\mu(\mathscr{T}_{uv})$ for every $v\in X^{*}$ and $u\in X^n$.
$\mu(\mathscr{T}_v\cap\mathscr{T}_{v'})=0$ for $v,v'\in X^n, v\neq v'$.
nodes.label: prop_measure lims propert

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10
nodes.statement: Let us show that $\mu(A)\geq |X|\mu(\tau_x(A))$ for any Borel set $A$. Consider sequences which represent points of the sets $A$ and $\tau_x(A)$: \[ \pi^{-1}_{\limGs[]}(A)=\bigcup_{g\in G}T_g\cdot g \ \ \Rightarrow \ \ \pi^{-1}_{\limGs[]}(\tau_x(A))=\bigcup_{g\in G}T_g g(x)\cdot g|_x. \] It implies \[ \mu(\tau_x(A))\leq \sum_{g\in G} \frac{1}{|X|}\mu_u (T_g)=\frac{1}{|X|}\mu(A). \] By applying this inequality $n$ times we get $|X|^n\mu(\mathscr{T}_v)=|X|^n\mu(\tau_v(\mathscr{T}))\leq\mu(\mathscr{T})$ for $v\in{X}^n$. Since $\mathscr{T}=\cup_{u\in X^n}\mathscr{T}_{u}$ we have that \[ \mu(\mathscr{T})\leq\sum_{u\in X^n}\mu(\mathscr{T}_{u})\leq\sum_{u\in X^n}\frac{1}{|X|^n}\mu(\mathscr{T})=\mu(\mathscr{T}). \] Hence all the above inequalities are actually equalities, $\mu(\mathscr{T})=|X|^n\mu(\mathscr{T}_{u})$ for every $u\in X^n$, and $\mu(\mathscr{T}_u\cap\mathscr{T}_{u'})=0$ for different $u,u'\in X^n$. Notice that since every Borel set $A\subset\mathscr{T}$ can be approximated by unions of tiles of the same level and using items 1 and 2 we have that if $\mu(\tau_x(A))<\varepsilon$ then $\mu(A)<\varepsilon|X|$. It is left to prove item 3. First, let us show that the assertion holds for the tiles $\mathscr{T}_v$. Since the measure $\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}$ is concentrated on the tile $\mathscr{T}$, up to sets of measure zero the set $\tau_x^{-1}(\mathscr{T}_v)$ is equal $\mathscr{T}_u$ if $v=ux$, and is empty if the last letter of $v$ is not $x$. Really, if $t\in\tau_x^{-1}(\mathscr{T}_{ux})$ and $t\in\mathscr{T}_v$ with $v\neq u, |v|=|u|$, then $\tau_x(t)\in\mathscr{T}_{vx}\cap\mathscr{T}_{ux}$ and the measure of such points is zero. Hence \[ \mu|_{\mathscr{T}}(\mathscr{T}_v)=\frac{1}{|X|}\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}(\mathscr{T}_u)=\sum_{x\in X} \frac{1}{|X|}\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}(\tau_x^{-1}(\mathscr{T}_v)). \] Now we can approximate any Borel set by unions of tiles and pass to the limit.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\mu(\tau_x(A))\le\mu(A)/|X|$, iterate and compare with $\mathscr{T}=\cup\mathscr{T}_u$ to force equalities; item 3 is checked on tiles and extended by approximation.

nodes.name: $\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}$ is Hutchinson's self-similar measure
nodes.statement: The tile $\mathscr{T}$ of the limit $G$-space $\limGs$ can be considered as the attractor of the iterated function system $\tau_x$, $x\in X$, i.e. \[ \mathscr{T}=\bigcup_{x\in X}\tau_x(\mathscr{T}). \] Hence Proposition~\ref{prop_measure lims propert} item~3 implies that $\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}$ is the self-similar measure on $\mathscr{T}$ by the standard definition of Hutchinson (\ref{eqn_self_similar_measure}). The measure $\mu$ is the $G$-invariant extension of the self-similar measure $\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}$ to the limit $G$-space $\limGs$.
nodes.statement_short: The tile is the attractor of the IFS $\{\tau_x\}$ and $\mu|_\mathscr{T}$ is its self-similar measure; $\mu$ is its $G$-invariant extension.

nodes.name: Graph $\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}$ of the nucleus
nodes.statement: Replacing each label $(x,y)$ by label $x$ in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ we get a strictly right-resolving graph denoted $\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}$ labeled by elements of $X$, so that we can apply the methods developed in Section~2.

nodes.name: Measure of the tile equals the measure number of the nucleus
nodes.statement: The measure $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ is equal to the measure number $meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})$ of the nucleus, in particular it is always integer. Moreover, $\mu(\mathscr{T})=1$ if and only if the action satisfies the open set condition.
nodes.statement_short: $\mu(\mathscr{T})=meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})$ is an integer, equal to 1 exactly under the open set condition.
conclusions: The measure $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ is equal to the measure number $meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})$ of the nucleus
in particular it is always integer.
Moreover, $\mu(\mathscr{T})=1$ if and only if the action satisfies the open set condition.
nodes.label: theor_tile_measure

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 11
nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} we have \[ \pi^{-1}_{\limGs[]}(\mathscr{T})=\bigcup_{g\in\mathcal{N}}F_g\cdot g^{-1}, \] where the sets $F_g$ are defined using the graph $\Gamma_\mathcal{N}$ (see Section~2). Thus \[ \mu(\mathscr{T})=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{N}}\mu_u(F_g)=meas(\mathcal{N}), \] which is integer by Theorem~\ref{theor_measure_graph_integer}. Observe that $\mu(\mathscr{T})\geq 1$ because $F_g=X^{-\omega}$ for $g=1\in\mathcal{N}$. If the action satisfies the open set condition then $\mu(\mathscr{T})=meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})=1$ by Corollary~\ref{cor_meas_sum_meas}. Suppose now that the action does not satisfy the open set condition. Then there exists an element $h$ of the nucleus, whose all restrictions are non-trivial. Let $\mathcal{N}_1$ be the set of all restrictions of $h$, and $\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}_1}$ be the corresponding graph. Then by Proposition~\ref{prop cup B_v eq cup F_v} \[ \sum_{g\in\mathcal{N}_1}\mu_u(F_g)=meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}_1})\geq 1. \] Thus $\mu(\mathscr{T})=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{N}}\mu_u(F_g)\geq meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}_1})+\mu_u(F_{g=1})\geq 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Pull back the tile to $\cup F_g\cdot g^{-1}$ via the nucleus, sum measures to get $meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})$; handle OSC and non-OSC cases separately.

nodes.name: Algorithmic computation of $\mu(\mathscr{T})$
nodes.statement: The measure $\mu(\mathscr{T})=meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})$ can be found algorithmically using the remarks after Proposition~\ref{prop_eigenvect_transition_matr}.

nodes.name: The tiles form a perfect multiple covering
nodes.statement: Every point $x\in\limGs$ is covered by at least $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles. The set $\dot{\limGs}$ of all points $x\in\limGs$, which are covered by exactly $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles, is open and dense in $\limGs$, and its complement has measure $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Every point lies in at least $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles, and the points in exactly $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles form an open dense conull set.
conclusions: Every point $x\in\limGs$ is covered by at least $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles.
The set $\dot{\limGs}$ of all points $x\in\limGs$, which are covered by exactly $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles, is open and dense in $\limGs$, and its complement has measure $0$.
nodes.label: points_above

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 12
nodes.statement: For each $x\in\limGs$ we define the number $n_x$ of such $g\in G$ that the tile $\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ contains $x$. First we prove the inequality. Let $x\in\limGs$ be represented by the pair $w\cdot g$ from $X^{-\omega}\times G$. Then $|V(w)|\geq meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})$ by Theorem~\ref{theor_measure_graph_integer}. If $h\in V(w)$ it means that the sequence $w$ ends in $h$, which by Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} means that there is a sequence $u_h\in X^{-\omega}$ such that $w$ is asymptotically equivalent to $u_h\cdot h$. It follows that $w\cdot g$ is asymptotically equivalent to $u_h\cdot hg$. It means, in turn, that $x$ belongs to the tile $\mathscr{T}\cdot hg$ for every $h\in V(w)$. It follows that $n_x\geq meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})$. Consider the set $\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{O}(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})$ defined in Lemma~\ref{lemma_set V open dense} using the graph $\Gamma_\mathcal{N}$, in other words $\mathcal{O}$ is the set of all $w\in X^{-\omega}$ that end in precisely $meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})$ elements of $\mathcal{N}$. By the same considerations as above we see that if $w\cdot g$ represents a point $x$ with $n_x=meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})$ then $|V(w)|=meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})$, that is, $w$ belongs to $\mathcal{O}$. In other words, the set $\mathcal{O}\times G$ is closed under the asymptotic equivalence relation on $X^{-\omega}\times G$, and it is the inverse image of the set $\dot{\limGs}$ under the factor map $\pi_{\limGs[]}$. Since the set $\mathcal{O}\times G$ is open and dense in $X^{-\omega}\times G$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma_set V open dense}, the same hold for $\dot{\limGs}$ in $\limGs$. The complement of $\dot{\limGs}$ has measure $0$, because the complement of the set $\mathcal{O}$ has measure $0$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma_set V open dense}.
nodes.statement_short: Each vertex in $V(w)$ yields a tile containing the point, so $n_x\ge meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})$; equality holds exactly over $\mathcal{O}\times G$, open dense and conull by Lemma 1.

nodes.name: The boundary of the tile has measure zero
nodes.statement: Let $\partial\mathscr{T}$ be the boundary of $\mathscr{T}$. Then $\mu(\partial\mathscr{T})=0$.
assumptions: Let $\partial\mathscr{T}$ be the boundary of $\mathscr{T}$.
conclusions: $\mu(\partial\mathscr{T})=0$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 13
nodes.statement: Take $x\in\partial\mathscr{T}$. Suppose that $x$ is covered by exactly $k=\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles. Let $U\subset\dot{\limGs}$ be the neighborhood of $x$ which intersects with finitely many tiles, say with $l\geq k$ tiles. By subtracting any tile that does not contain $x$ we may suppose that $l=k$, that is, $U$ has nonempty intersection only with those tiles that contain $x$. Now, since $x$ is in the boundary of $\mathscr{T}$, there is a point $x'$ in $U$ that is not covered by $\mathscr{T}$ (otherwise $x\in U\subset\mathscr{T}$), thus $x'$ is covered by less than $k$ tiles, contradiction. Hence $\partial\mathscr{T}$ is in the complement of $\dot{\limGs}$ and has measure $0$.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: a boundary point covered by exactly $k$ tiles would have nearby points covered by fewer than $k$ tiles.

nodes.name: Measure of the intersection of two tiles
nodes.statement: Two tiles $\mathscr{T}\cdot g_1$ and $\mathscr{T}\cdot g_2$ for $g_1,g_2\in G$ have nonempty intersection if and only if $g_1g_2^{-1}\in\mathcal{N}$. Let us show how to find the measure of this intersection. By Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} we have \begin{eqnarray*} \pi^{-1}_{\limGs[]}((\mathscr{T}\cdot g_1)\cap (\mathscr{T}\cdot g_2))=\bigcup_{{\scriptsize\begin{array}{c} h_1,h_2\in\mathcal{N} \\ g_1g_2^{-1}=h_1h_2^{-1} \end{array}}} (F_{h_1}\cap F_{h_2})\cdot h_1^{-1}g_1, \end{eqnarray*} where the sets $F_g$ are defined using the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$. The word problem in contracting self-similar groups is solvable in polynomial time \cite[Proposition~2.13.10]{self_sim_groups} (one can use the program package \cite{AutomGrp}). The measures of intersections $F_{h_1}\cap F_{h_2}$ can be found for example using method described after Corollary~\ref{cor_meas_gr_rational}.
nodes.statement_short: $\mu((\mathscr{T}g_1)\cap(\mathscr{T}g_2))$ is computed from measures of $F_{h_1}\cap F_{h_2}$ over nucleus pairs with $h_1h_2^{-1}=g_1g_2^{-1}$.
nodes.label: rem_meas_inters_tiles

nodes.name: When can the open set condition be achieved?
nodes.statement: It is an interesting open question in what cases we can always choose a self-similar action which satisfies the open set condition (see \cite{mult_an_self_sim,lag_wang:haar} for the abelian case and applications to wavelets).

nodes.name: The measure $\mu$ depends only on the virtual endomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $\phi: H\rightarrow G$ be a virtual endomorphism of the group $G$. Let $(G,X^*)$ and $(G,Y^*)$ be the contracting self-similar actions defined respectively by the triples $(\phi,T,C)$ and $(\phi,T',C')$. Then the homeomorphism $\alpha : \limGs[(G,X^*)]\longrightarrow \limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ from Theorem~\ref{theor_limsX hom limsY} preserves measure, i.e. \[ \mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(A))=\mu_{(G,X^*)}(A) \] for any Borel set $A$.
nodes.statement_short: The homeomorphism $\alpha$ between limit $G$-spaces of two actions with the same virtual endomorphism preserves $\mu$.
assumptions: Let $\phi: H\rightarrow G$ be a virtual endomorphism of the group $G$.
Let $(G,X^*)$ and $(G,Y^*)$ be the contracting self-similar actions defined respectively by the triples $(\phi,T,C)$ and $(\phi,T',C')$.
conclusions: Then the homeomorphism $\alpha : \limGs[(G,X^*)]\longrightarrow \limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ from Theorem~\ref{theor_limsX hom limsY} preserves measure
nodes.label: theor_measure_limGs_invariant

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 14
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{N}$ be the nucleus and $\mathscr{T}$ be the tile of the action $(G,X^{*})$. By Theorem~\ref{theor_tile_measure} and Theorem~\ref{theor_measure_graph_integer} \begin{equation} \mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T})=meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})=\min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} |V(w)|=k\in\mathbb{N}, \end{equation} where $V(w)$ is defined using the graph $\Gamma_\mathcal{N}$. Consider \[ \pi_Y^{-1}(\alpha(\mathscr{T}))=\bigcup_{g\in G} T_g\cdot g\quad (\mbox{here } T_g\subseteq Y^{-\omega}), \] where $\pi_Y:Y^{-\omega}\times G\rightarrow \limGs$ is the canonical projection. Take $w\in Y^{-\omega}$ and let us prove that there exist at least $k$ elements $g\in G$ such that $w\in T_g$. The tiles $\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ cover the limit $G$-space $\limGs[(G,X^*)]$, and we can find $g\in G$ such that if $x=\alpha^{-1}(y)$ for $y=\pi_{Y}(w\cdot g)\in\limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ then $x$ belongs to the tile $\mathscr{T}$. Then $x$ is represented by the sequence $u\cdot 1$ for $u\in X^{-\omega}$. Equation~(\ref{eqn_theor_meraXY_mu tile }) implies $|V(u)|\geq k$ and so there exist $k$ elements $h_1,\ldots, h_k\in\mathcal{N}$ and sequences $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in X^{-\omega}$ such that for every $i$ there exists a left-infinite path in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ which ends in $h_i$ and is labeled by $(u,u_i)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} \[ x=\pi_X(u\cdot 1)=\pi_X(u_i\cdot h_i)\quad\mbox{ and }\quad x\cdot h_i^{-1}\in\mathscr{T} \] for every $i=1,\ldots, k$. Then \[ \pi_Y(w\cdot gh_i^{-1})=\pi_Y(w\cdot g)h_i^{-1}=y\cdot h_i^{-1}=\alpha(x\cdot h_i^{-1})\in\alpha(\mathscr{T}) \] and thus $w\in T_{gh_i^{-1}}$ for all $i=1,\ldots, k$. Let $\chi_{T_g}$ be the characteristic function of the set $T_g$. Then $\sum_{g\in G}\chi_{T_g}(x)\geq k$ for almost all $x$. Integrating we get $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\mathscr{T}))=\sum_{g\in G} \mu_u(T_g)\geq k=\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T})$. Let us now show that $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\mathscr{T}_v))\leq\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T}_v)$ for any $v\in X^*$. Indeed, let $n=|v|$, then it follows from Theorem \ref{theor_limsX hom limsY} that $\alpha(\mathscr{T}_v)=\alpha(\tau_v(\mathscr{T}))=\tau_u(\alpha(\mathscr{T}))g$ for some word $u\in Y^n$ and $g\in G$. Thus \begin{eqnarray*} \mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\mathscr{T}_v))&=&\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\tau_u(\alpha(\mathscr{T})))\leq\frac{1}{|X|^n}\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\mathscr{T}))=\\ &=&\frac{1}{|X|^n}\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T})=\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T}_v). \end{eqnarray*} Let us prove that $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu_{(G,X^*)}$. Indeed, let $\mu_{(G,X^*)}(A)<\varepsilon$, $\pi^{-1}_{X}(A)=\cup_g T_g\cdot g$. Then $\sum_g\mu_u(T_g)<\varepsilon$. It follows that there exist $v_{i,g}\in X^*$ such that $T_g\subset\cup_iX^{-\omega} v_{i,g}$ and $\sum_{i,g}|X|^{-|v_{i,g}|}<\varepsilon$. Then $A\subset\cup_{i,g}\mathscr{T}_{v_{i,g}}\cdot g$, and we have that $\sum_{i,g}\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T}_{v_{i,g}})<\varepsilon\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T})$. Then $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(A))\leq\sum\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\mathscr{T}_{v_{i,g}}))\leq\sum\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T}_{v_{i,g}})<\varepsilon\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T})$. Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, we are done. We will now prove that $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha\leq\mu_{(G,X^*)}$. Since both $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha$ and $\mu_{(G,X^*)}$ are invariant under multiplication by $g\in G$ it suffices to prove this inequality for sets $A\subset\mathscr{T}$. Since any Borel $A$ is a union of a closed set and a set of arbitrarily small measure, it suffices to prove the inequality for closed sets, as $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu_{(G,X^*)}$ by above. So let $A\subset\mathscr{T}$ be a closed set. For each $n$, let $A_n$ be the union of all tiles $\mathscr{T}_v,v\in X^n,$ that have non-empty intersection with $A$. Let us show that $A=\cap_n A_n$. Suppose $x\in\cap A_n$, and $x$ is not in $A$. Then for each $n$ there is $v_n\in X^n$ such that $\mathscr{T}_{v_n}$ has nonempty intersection with $A$ and $x\in\mathscr{T}_{v_n}$. It follows that $x$ has some representation $u_nv_n\in X^{-\omega}$. Since the number of such representations is finite, we may choose subsequence $n_k$ such that $v_{n_k}$ is the beginning of some word $v\in X^{-\omega}$. Since $A$ is compact it follows that $A$ has nonempty intersection with $\cap_k\mathscr{T}_{v_{n_k}}$, thus $\cap_k\mathscr{T}_{v_{n_k}}$ contains at least two points, which is impossible. Since $A_n$ is the union of some tiles of level $n$, which are disjoint up to sets of measure $0$, the inequality also holds for all $A_n$. Going to the limit, we get the inequality for $A$. By interchanging $X$ and $Y$ we get the reverse inequality, and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound $\mu_Y(\alpha(\mathscr{T}))\ge k$ by counting nucleus paths, upper bound on subtiles, absolute continuity, then approximation of closed sets by tile unions; symmetry in $X,Y$ finishes.

nodes.name: $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ as minimal $|V(w)|$
nodes.statement: \mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T})=meas(\Gamma_\mathcal{N})=\min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} |V(w)|=k\in\mathbb{N},
nodes.label: eqn_theor_meraXY_mu tile

nodes.name: Uniform weight is essential in Theorem 14
nodes.statement: It is important in the theorem that we take the uniform Bernoulli measure on $X^{-\omega}$. The problem is that the homeomorphism $\alpha$ may change the Bernoulli measure with a non-uniform weight to a measure that is not Bernoulli.

nodes.name: Self-similar measure $\mathsf{m}$ on the limit space
nodes.statement: The push-forward of the uniform Bernoulli measure $\mu_u$ under the factor map $\pi_{\lims[]}:X^{-\omega}\rightarrow\lims$ defines the \textit{self-similar measure $\mathsf{m}$ on the limit space} $\lims$.
nodes.definiendum: self-similar measure $\mathsf{m}$ on the limit space

nodes.name: The shift preserves $\mathsf{m}$
nodes.statement: The shift $\mathsf{s}$ is a measure-preserving transformation of $\lims$.
conclusions: The shift $\mathsf{s}$ is a measure-preserving transformation of $\lims$.

nodes.name: Set $\mathcal{U}$
nodes.statement: Consider the set $\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{N})$ of all sequences $w\in X^{-\omega}$ with the property that every left-infinite path in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(w,w)$ ends in $1$.

nodes.name: Set $\mathcal{U}^*$
nodes.statement: Define $\mathcal{U}^*$ as the set of finite words that satisfy the same condition.

nodes.name: The set $\mathcal{U}$ is open, dense, of full measure and saturated
nodes.statement: The set $\mathcal{U}$ is open and dense in $X^{-\omega}$, and $\mu_p(\mathcal{U})=1$. For each $w\in \mathcal{U}$ there is a beginning of $w$ that belongs to $\mathcal{U}^*$, and $\mathcal{U}=\cup_{w\in\mathcal{U}^*}X^{-\omega} w$. The sets $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{U}\times G$ are closed under the asymptotic equivalence relation on $X^{-\omega}$ and $X^{-\omega}\times G$ respectively.
conclusions: The set $\mathcal{U}$ is open and dense in $X^{-\omega}$, and $\mu_p(\mathcal{U})=1$.
The sets $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{U}\times G$ are closed under the asymptotic equivalence relation on $X^{-\omega}$ and $X^{-\omega}\times G$ respectively.
nodes.label: lemma U_open_dense_meas1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Construct the graph $\Gamma$ with the elements of $\mathcal{N}$ as vertices, for each edge labeled by $(x,x)$ in $\mathcal{N}$ we have the edge in $\Gamma$ with the same starting and end vertices, and labeled by $x$; and for each edge in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(x,y)$ for $x\neq y$ there is an edge in $\Gamma$ with the same starting vertex that ends in the trivial element and labeled by $x$. Then the set $\mathcal{U}$ coincides with the set $\mathcal{O}(\Gamma)$. Indeed, $h\in V_{\Gamma}(w)$ if and only if there is a path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(w,w)$ that ends in $h$, thus $w\in\mathcal{U}$ if and only if $V_{\Gamma}(w)=\{1\}$. For every nontrivial element $h\in\mathcal{N}$ there exists a word $v\in X^{*}$ such that $h(v)\neq v$. It follows that there exists a path in the graph $\Gamma$ from $h$ to $1$. Hence the component $\{1\}$ is the only strongly connected component of the graph $\Gamma$ without outgoing edges. By Corollary~\ref{cor_meas_sum_meas} the measure number of $\Gamma$ is $1$, and $\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{O}(\Gamma)$. The first statement of the lemma now follows from Lemma~\ref{lemma_set V open dense}. Let us show that the set $\mathcal{U}$ is closed under the asymptotic equivalence relation (then the set $\mathcal{U}\times G$ is also closed). It is sufficient to show that if there is a path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(u,v)$ and $u\in\mathcal{U}$ ($v\in\mathcal{U}$) then $v\in\mathcal{U}$ ($u\in\mathcal{U}$). Let the path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(u,v)$ end in $h$. It follows that $u$ is asymptotically equivalent to $v\cdot h$. Suppose there is a path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(v,v)$ that ends in $g$. It follows that $v$ is asymptotically equivalent to $v\cdot g$. Thus $u$ is asymptotically equivalent to $v\cdot gh$ which is asymptotically equivalent to $u\cdot h^{-1}gh$. By definition, there is a path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(u,u)$ which ends in $h^{-1}gh$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}$ we get $h^{-1}gh=1$, thus $g=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Realize $\mathcal{U}$ as $\mathcal{O}(\Gamma)$ for an auxiliary graph with measure number 1 and apply Lemma 1; saturation via conjugating nucleus paths.

nodes.name: Almost every point has $|X|$ preimages
nodes.statement: Almost every point of $\lims$ has precisely $|X|$ preimages under~$\mathsf{s}$.
conclusions: Almost every point of $\lims$ has precisely $|X|$ preimages under~$\mathsf{s}$.
nodes.label: prop_measure_prop_lims

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 15
nodes.statement: Since every point of $\lims$ has at most $|X|$ preimages under $\mathsf{s}$, it is enough to show that for almost every $w\in X^{-\omega}$ the map $\pi_{\lims[]}:\sigma^{-1}(w)\rightarrow\mathsf{s}^{-1}(\pi_{\lims[]}(w))$ is one-to-one. Suppose that for some $w\in X^{-\omega}$ and $x\neq y$ in $X$ we have $\pi_{\lims[]}(wx)=\pi_{\lims[]}(wy)$. It follows that $wx,wy$ are asymptotically equivalent, thus there is a left-infinite path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(wx,wy)$. It follows that the prefix of this path labeled by $(w,w)$ must end in the nontrivial element, so $w\not\in\mathcal{U}$. Since $\mu_u(\mathcal{U})=1$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma U_open_dense_meas1}, we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Collapsing preimages forces a nontrivial nucleus path on $(w,w)$, so $w\notin\mathcal{U}$, a null set by Lemma 2.

nodes.name: Tiles over $\mathcal{U}^*$ embed in the limit space
nodes.statement: Let $\rho$ be the factor map $\limGs\rightarrow\lims$. Then for any $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ the restriction $\rho|_{\mathscr{T}_u}:\mathscr{T}_u\rightarrow\mathsf{T}_u$ is a homeomorphism, $\rho^{-1}(\mathsf{T}_u)=\sqcup_{g\in G}\mathscr{T}_u\cdot g$.
assumptions: Let $\rho$ be the factor map $\limGs\rightarrow\lims$.
for any $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$
conclusions: the restriction $\rho|_{\mathscr{T}_u}:\mathscr{T}_u\rightarrow\mathsf{T}_u$ is a homeomorphism
$\rho^{-1}(\mathsf{T}_u)=\sqcup_{g\in G}\mathscr{T}_u\cdot g$.
nodes.label: x_j_homeo

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 16
nodes.statement: By definition, the map $\rho|_{\mathscr{T}_u}:\mathscr{T}_u\rightarrow\mathsf{T}_u$ is surjective, and $\mathscr{T}_u$ is compact. Hence in order to prove that $\rho$ is a homeomorphism it is left to show that $\rho$ is injective on $\mathscr{T}_u$. Take $x,y\in\mathscr{T}_u$, and let $wu\in X^{-\omega}$ represent $x$ and $vu\in X^{-\omega}$ represent $y$. Suppose that $\rho(x)=\rho(y)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} it means that there is a left-infinite path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(wu,vu)$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$, this path must end in $1$. It follows, that $wu$ and $vu$ represent the same point of the tile $\mathscr{T}_u$, and $x=y$. To prove the second claim, take $x\in\mathscr{T}_u\cdot g\cap\mathscr{T}_u\cdot g'$. Then $x$ is represented by two asymptotically equivalent sequences $wu\cdot g$ and $w'u\cdot g'$. It follows that there is a path in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(u,u)$ which ends in $g'g^{-1}$. Then $g=g'$ since $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Compact-to-Hausdorff continuous surjection; injectivity and disjointness because nucleus paths over $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ end in 1.

nodes.name: The projection to the limit space is a covering mod null sets
nodes.statement: The projection $\limGs\rightarrow\lims$ is a covering map up to sets of measure zero.
conclusions: The projection $\limGs\rightarrow\lims$ is a covering map up to sets of measure zero.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 17
nodes.statement: Consider the sets $\tilde{\limGs}=\pi_{\limGs[]}(\mathcal{U}\times G)$ and $\tilde{\lims}=\pi_{\lims[]}(\mathcal{U})$. It follows that $\tilde{\limGs}/G=\tilde{\lims}$. Since the set $\mathcal{U}$ has measure $1$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma U_open_dense_meas1}, the complements of $\mathcal{U}\times G$, of $\tilde{\limGs}$, and of $\tilde{\lims}$ have measure $0$. Since the group $G$ acts properly on $\limGs$, the same holds for $\tilde{\limGs}$. It is left to prove the freeness. Suppose $x\cdot g=x$ for $x\in\tilde{\limGs}$ and $g\in G$. Let $u\cdot h$ be a representative of $x$ in $X^{-\omega}\times G$. It follows that $u\cdot hg$ is asymptotically equivalent to $u\cdot h$, thus there is a path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(u,u)$ that ends in $h^{-1}gh$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}$ we have $g=1$. Hence the projection $\tilde{\limGs}\rightarrow\tilde{\lims}$ is a covering map, and the statement follows.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to the conull saturated set given by $\mathcal{U}$, where the proper $G$-action is also free, hence a covering.

nodes.name: Quotient measure
nodes.statement:
Let $(\limGs[],
u)$ be a locally compact measure space, the group $G$ acts freely and properly discontinuously on $\limGs[]$ by homeomorphisms, and the measure $
u$ is $G$-invariant. There is a unique measure $
u_{*}$ on the quotient space $\limGs[]/G$, called the 	extit{quotient measure}, with the property that if $U$ is an open subset of $\limGs[]$ such that $Ug\cap Uh=\emptyset$ for all $g,h\in G$, $g
eq h$, then $
u_{*}(U/G)=
u(U)$.
nodes.statement_short: For a free properly discontinuous measure-preserving $G$-action, the unique measure on $X/G$ agreeing with $\nu$ on wandering open sets.

nodes.name: Quotient of $\mu$ is $\mathsf{m}$
nodes.statement: The quotient measure $\mu_{*}$ of the limit $G$-space $(\limGs,\mu)$ coincides with the measure $\mathsf{m}$ on the limit space $\lims$.
conclusions: The quotient measure $\mu_{*}$ of the limit $G$-space $(\limGs,\mu)$ coincides with the measure $\mathsf{m}$ on the limit space $\lims$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 18
nodes.statement: Consider the sets $\tilde{\lims}$ and $\tilde{\limGs}$ of full measure from the previous theorem. For every $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ we have $\mathsf{T}_u\subset\tilde{\lims}$, $\mathscr{T}_u\cdot g\subset\tilde{\limGs}$ for every $g\in G$, and $\rho^{-1}(\mathsf{T}_u)=\bigsqcup_{g\in G} \mathscr{T}_u\cdot g$ by Proposition~\ref{x_j_homeo}. Since $\tilde{\lims}=\cup_{u\in\mathcal{U}^*}\mathsf{T}_u$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma U_open_dense_meas1} it suffices to show that for any $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ the restriction of $\mu_{*}$ on $\mathsf{T}_u$ is equal to the restriction of $\mathsf{m}$. Take a Borel set $A\subset\mathscr{T}_u$ and consider its preimage $\pi^{-1}_{\limGs[]}(A)=\sqcup_{g\in\mathcal{N}} A_g\cdot g$. Then $\pi^{-1}_{\lims[]}(\rho(A))=\sqcup_{g\in\mathcal{N}} A_g$. Here the union is disjoint because if $w\in{A_g\cap{}A_h}$ then $w\cdot g$ and $w\cdot h$ are asymptotically equivalent to $vu$ and $v'u$ respectively, for some $v,v'\in X^{-\omega}$. It follows that $vu\cdot g^{-1}$ is equivalent to $v'u\cdot h^{-1}$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}$, $g=h$. Hence \[ \mathsf{m}(\rho(A))=\mu_u(\pi^{-1}_{\lims[]}(\rho(A)))=\mu_u(\sqcup_{g\in\mathcal{N}} A_g)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{N}}\mu_u(A_g). \] By the property of the quotient measure \[ \mu_{*}(\rho(A))=\mu(A)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{N}}\mu_u(A_g)=\mathsf{m}(\rho(A)). \]
nodes.statement_short: Check equality on tiles $\mathsf{T}_u$, $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$, which cover a conull set, by computing both measures on preimages.

nodes.name: The measure space $(\mathscr{J}_G,\mathsf{m})$ depends only on the virtual endomorphism
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{theor_measure_limGs_invariant} holds for the limit space $\lims$, i.e. the measure space $(\lims,\mathsf{m})$ depends only on the associated virtual endomorphism.

nodes.name: Measure of tiles $\mathsf{T}_u$ for $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$
nodes.statement: $\mathsf{m}(\mathsf{T}_u)=\mu(\mathscr{T}_u)=\frac{1}{|X|^{|u|}}meas(\mathscr{T})$ for $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$.
assumptions: for $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$
conclusions: $\mathsf{m}(\mathsf{T}_u)=\mu(\mathscr{T}_u)=\frac{1}{|X|^{|u|}}meas(\mathscr{T})$

nodes.name: Limit dynamical system is Bernoulli
nodes.statement: $(\lims,\mathsf{s},\mathsf{m})$ is conjugate to the one-sided Bernoulli $|X|$-shift.
conclusions: $(\lims,\mathsf{s},\mathsf{m})$ is conjugate to the one-sided Bernoulli $|X|$-shift.
nodes.label: theor_lims_conju_Bernoulli

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 21
nodes.statement: We will use notions and results from \cite{hoffman:Bernoulli}. First recall that a measure preserving map with entropy $\log{d}$ is called {\it uniformly $d$-to-one endomorphism} if it is almost everywhere $d$-to-one and the conditional expectation of each preimage is $1/d$. The standard example is $(X^{-\omega},\sigma,\mu_u)$, which is uniformly $|X|$-to-one. Next we want to show that $(\lims,\mathsf{s},\mathsf{m})$ is also uniformly $|X|$-to-one. By Proposition~\ref{prop_measure_prop_lims} the map $\pi:X^{-\omega}\rightarrow\lims$ is injective on the preimages $\sigma^{-1}(w)$ for almost all $w\in X^{-\omega}$, that is, $\pi$ is {\it tree adapted} in terminology of \cite{hoffman:Bernoulli}. We can apply Lemma~2.3 from \cite{hoffman:Bernoulli}, which says that a tree adapted factor of a uniform $d$-to-one endomorphism is again uniform $d$-to-one endomorphism. In particular, the shift $\mathsf{s}$ is the map of maximal entropy $\log |X|$. To prove the theorem, we use the following Theorem~5.5 in \cite{hoffman:Bernoulli}. \begin{theor} A uniform $d$-to-one endomorphism $(Y,S,\mu)$ is one-sidedly conjugated to the one-sided Bernoulli $d$-shift if and only if there exists a generating function $f$ so that $(Y,S,\mu)$ and $f$ are tree very weak Bernoulli. \end{theor} Recall the definition of tree very weak Bernoulli and generating function.
